```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(vegan)
```

# Genotype-Environment Associations 

**Summary**: In this script, we use several methods to identify loci that may be associated with environmental gradients. We perform each analysis in parallel: one in the native range and one in the introduced range. 

## RDA: Redundancy Analysis 

RDA determines how groups of loci covary in response to the multivariate environment, and can detect processes that result in weak, multilocus molecular signatures. RDA is a two-step analysis in which genetic and environmental data are analyzed using multivariate linear regression, producing a matrix of fitted values. Then PCA of the fitted values is used to produce canonical axes, which are linear combinations of the predictors. (From Reatini et al., in prep)


### Western United States 
**Summary**: After selecting only the samples in the Western United States, there is only 11% missing data in the genetic dataset. Very little of the variation appears to be explained by the genetic component (about 2%). There are 80 candidate SNPs from the first 3 RDA axes. 

```{r}
# load in dataframe with pop env vars for each individual for the individual-based GEA
env <- read.delim("individual_climate_data_30s.txt", sep = " ")
env$Site <- as.character(env$Site)

# Filter for individuals/pops in the GEA dataset 
locations <- read.delim("EUVI_locations.txt", header =T)
# Filter locations to only samples that we are using: 
popmap3 <- read.delim("samples_to_keep.txt", sep = " ")
locations_update <- distinct(locations[locations$EUVI_Sample %in% popmap3$V1,])

# Filter to all samples we are keeping: 
env <- env[env$EUVI_Sample %in% locations_update$EUVI_Sample,]

# Now filter to only include samples in the introduced range and only the variables we are interested in
env_WUS <- env %>% 
  dplyr::filter(Long < 0) %>% 
  dplyr::select(EUVI_Sample, Site, Lat, Long, bio5, bio6, bio19, bio17, bio2) %>% 
  arrange(EUVI_Sample)
predictors <- env_WUS[,5:9]

# Prepare genotype data
WUS_genos <- read.table("introduced.populations.snps.thinned.1SD-removed.noLAFI.maf0.01.NoExHet.plink.raw", header = T, sep =" ", row.names=1)
dim(WUS_genos)

# extract genotypes from dataframe for prelim analysis
WUS_genos_only <- WUS_genos[,6:7092]

# calculate amount of missing data
sum(is.na(WUS_genos_only))/(7087*202) # the denominator is the sites*N

# fill missing values (NAs) with overall average for allele frequency variation
WUS_genos.imp <- apply(WUS_genos_only, 2, function(x) replace(x, is.na(x), as.numeric(names(which.max(table(x))))))
# double check that there are no longer any NA values
sum(is.na(WUS_genos.imp)) 
# genotype data is ready! 

# Need to make sure that predictors are in the same order as the genotype data! 
# I fixed this by arrganging by the sample name prior to generating the predictor dataframe

WUS.rda <- rda(WUS_genos.imp ~ ., data = predictors, scale = T)
WUS.rda

# calculate adjusted r^2
RsquareAdj(WUS.rda) # constrained ordination explains 2% of the genotypic variation

# print eigenvalue summary and plot it
summary(eigenvals(WUS.rda, model = "constrained"))
screeplot(WUS.rda)

# plot RDA results for individuals

# axes 1 & 2
plot(WUS.rda, type="n", scaling=3)
points(WUS.rda, display="sites", pch=21, cex=1.75, col="black", scaling=3) 
text(WUS.rda, scaling=3, display="bp", col="black", cex=1.2)        
#legend("topright", legend=levels(eco), bty="n", col="black", pch=21, cex=1.4, pt.bg=bg)

# axes 1 & 3
plot(WUS.rda, type="n", scaling=3, choices=c(1,3))
points(WUS.rda, display="sites", pch=21, cex=1.75, col="black", scaling=3, choices=c(1,3)) 
text(WUS.rda, scaling=3, display="bp", col="black", cex=1.2, choices=c(1,3))

# extract loadings of SNPs in ordination space
load.rda <- scores(WUS.rda, choices=c(1:3), display="species")

# Now extract the SNPs with absolute value of loadings of the 95 percentile of all the SNPs, which 
# is then weighted based on the eigenvalues of each RDA axis 

# about 41% of the top 5% of SNPs should be from the first axis based on the eigenvalue (54.77 of 131.69 (sum of the first three axes)), 41% of the top 5% of SNPs (354) is ~ 145 SNPs, about 2% of the total SNPs, etc. 
cand1 <- which(abs(load.rda[,1]) >= quantile(abs(load.rda[,1]), 0.98)) 
cand2 <- which(abs(load.rda[,2]) >= quantile(abs(load.rda[,2]), 0.985)) # 31% of 5%, ~110 SNPs
cand3 <- which(abs(load.rda[,3]) >= quantile(abs(load.rda[,3]), 0.987)) # 27% of 5%, ~96 SNPs

# Total number of outlier SNPs
ncand <- length(cand1) + length(cand2) + length(cand3) #345 candidate snps in Western United States 

# make dataframe with candidate SNPs and correlations with each env variable
cand1 <- cbind.data.frame(rep(1,times=length(cand1)), names(cand1), unname(cand1))
cand2 <- cbind.data.frame(rep(2,times=length(cand2)), names(cand2), unname(cand2))
cand3 <- cbind.data.frame(rep(3,times=length(cand3)), names(cand3), unname(cand3))

colnames(cand1) <- colnames(cand2) <- colnames(cand3) <- c("axis","snp","loading")

cand <- rbind(cand1, cand2, cand3)
cand$snp <- as.character(cand$snp)
cand <- unique(cand)

foo <- matrix(nrow=(ncand), ncol=5)  # 5 columns for 5 predictors
colnames(foo) <- c("bio5","bio6","bio19","bio17","bio2")

for (i in 1:length(cand$snp)) {
  nam <- cand[i,2]
  snp.gen <- WUS_genos.imp[,nam]
  foo[i,] <- apply(predictors,2,function(x) cor(x,snp.gen))
}

cand <- cbind.data.frame(cand,foo) 
cand_WUS <- cand

# check which of the predictors each SNP is most strongly correlated with
for (i in 1:length(cand$snp)) {
  bar <- cand[i,]
  cand[i,9] <- names(which.max(abs(bar[4:8]))) # gives the variable
  cand[i,10] <- max(abs(bar[4:8]))              # gives the correlation
}

colnames(cand)[9] <- "predictor"
colnames(cand)[10] <- "correlation"

Env_Predictors <- levels(as.factor(cand$predictor))
No_Snps <- as.numeric(table(cand$predictor))
piedata <- data.frame(Env_Predictors,No_Snps)

# pie chart 
ggplot(piedata, aes(x="", y=No_Snps, fill=Env_Predictors)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c('#1f78b4','#33a02c','#e31a1c','#ffff33','gold')) +
  geom_col(color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = No_Snps),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5)) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  ggtitle("Number of candidate SNPs per environmental predictor") +
  theme_void()

# plot!
sel <- cand$snp
env <- cand$predictor
env[env=="bio5"] <- '#1f78b4'
env[env=="bio6"] <- '#33a02c'
env[env=="bio19"] <- '#e31a1c'
env[env=="bio17"] <- '#ffff33'
env[env=="bio2"] <- 'gold'
                
# color by predictor:
col.pred <- rownames(WUS.rda$CCA$v) # pull the SNP names
              
for (i in 1:length(sel)) {           # color code candidate SNPs
  foo <- match(sel[i],col.pred)
  col.pred[foo] <- env[i]
}
              
col.pred[grep("X",col.pred)] <- '#f1eef6' # non-candidate SNPs
empty <- col.pred
empty[grep("#f1eef6",empty)] <- rgb(0,1,0, alpha=0) # transparent
empty.outline <- ifelse(empty=="#00FF0000","#00FF0000","gray32")
bg <- c('#e31a1c','gold','red4','#ffff33','#1f78b4','#33a02c')

# axes 1 & 2
plot(WUS.rda, type="n", scaling=3, xlim=c(-1,1), ylim=c(-1,1))
points(WUS.rda, display="species", pch=21, cex=1.3, col="gray32", bg=col.pred, scaling=3)
points(WUS.rda, display="species", pch=21, cex=1.3, col=empty.outline, bg=empty, scaling=3)
text(WUS.rda, scaling=3, display="bp", col="black", cex=1.2)
#legend("bottomright", legend=c("TEMPannual","TEMPseasonality","TEMPmax","TEMPdriestquarter","PPTannual","PPTseasonality"), bty="n", col="black", pch=21, cex=1, pt.bg=bg)

# axes 1 & 3
plot(WUS.rda, type="n", scaling=3, xlim=c(-1,1), ylim=c(-1,1), choices=c(1,3))
points(WUS.rda, display="species", pch=21, cex=1.3, col="gray32", bg=col.pred, scaling=3, choices=c(1,3))
points(WUS.rda, display="species", pch=21, cex=1.3, col=empty.outline, bg=empty, scaling=3, choices=c(1,3))
text(WUS.rda, scaling=3, display="bp", col="black", cex=1.2, choices=c(1,3))
#legend("bottomright", legend=c("TEMPannual","TEMPseasonality","TEMPmax","TEMPdriestquarter","PPTannual","PPTseasonality"), bty="n", col="black", pch=21, cex=1.2, pt.bg=bg)

```

## Native range: Turkey and Greece 
**Summary**: After selecting only the samples in the native range (Turkey + Greece), there is only 12% missing data in the genetic dataset. Very little of the variation appears to be explained by the genetic component (about 2%). There are 60 candidate SNPs from the first 3 RDA axes, and over half of the candidates are associated with Bio2.


```{r}
# Now filter to only include samples in the introduced range and only the variables we are interested in
env <- read.delim("individual_climate_data_30s.txt", sep = " ")
env$Site <- as.character(env$Site)

env_EU <- env %>% 
  dplyr::filter(Long > 0) %>% 
  dplyr::select(EUVI_Sample, Site, Lat, Long, bio5, bio6, bio19, bio17, bio2) %>% 
  arrange(EUVI_Sample)

predictors <- env_EU[,5:9]
# Prepare genotype data

EU_genos <- read.table("native.populations.snps.thinned.1SD-removed.noLAFI.maf0.01.NoExHet.plink.raw", header = T, sep =" ", row.names=1)
dim(EU_genos)

# extract genotypes from dataframe for prelim analysis
EU_genos_only <- EU_genos[,6:7092]

# calculate amount of missing data
sum(is.na(EU_genos_only))/(7087*101) # the denominator is the sites*N

# fill missing values (NAs) with overall average for allele frequency variation
EU_genos.imp <- apply(EU_genos_only, 2, function(x) replace(x, is.na(x), as.numeric(names(which.max(table(x))))))
# double check that there are no longer any NA values
sum(is.na(EU_genos.imp)) 
# genotype data is ready! 

EU.rda <- rda(EU_genos.imp ~ ., data = predictors, scale = T)
EU.rda

# calculate adjusted r^2
RsquareAdj(EU.rda) # constrained ordination explains 5% of the genotypic variation

# print eigenvalue summary and plot it
summary(eigenvals(EU.rda, model = "constrained"))
screeplot(EU.rda)

# plot RDA results for individuals

# axes 1 & 2

points(EU.rda, display="sites", pch=21, cex=1.75, col="black", scaling=3) 
text(EU.rda, scaling=3, display="bp", col="black", cex=1.2)        
#legend("topright", legend=levels(eco), bty="n", col="black", pch=21, cex=1.4, pt.bg=bg)

# axes 1 & 3
plot(EU.rda, type="n", scaling=3, choices=c(1,3))
points(EU.rda, display="sites", pch=21, cex=1.75, col="black", scaling=3, choices=c(1,3))

# extract loadings of SNPs in ordination space

# Now extract the SNPs with absolute value of loadings of the 95 percentile of all the SNPs, which 
# is then weighted based on the eigenvalues of each RDA axis 

# about 67% of the top 5% of SNPs should be from the first axis based on the eigenvalue (361.2 of 534.3 (sum of the first three axes)), 67% of the top 5% of SNPs (354) is ~ 237 SNPs, about 3.3% of the total SNPs, etc. 
cand1 <- which(abs(load.rda[,1]) >= quantile(abs(load.rda[,1]), 0.966))
cand2 <- which(abs(load.rda[,2]) >= quantile(abs(load.rda[,2]), 0.99))
cand3 <- which(abs(load.rda[,3]) >= quantile(abs(load.rda[,3]), 0.994))

# Total number of outlier SNPs
ncand <- length(cand1) + length(cand2) + length(cand3) #355 candidate snps in Western United States 

# make dataframe with candidate SNPs and correlations with each env variable
cand1 <- cbind.data.frame(rep(1,times=length(cand1)), names(cand1), unname(cand1))
cand2 <- cbind.data.frame(rep(2,times=length(cand2)), names(cand2), unname(cand2))
cand3 <- cbind.data.frame(rep(3,times=length(cand3)), names(cand3), unname(cand3))

colnames(cand1) <- colnames(cand2) <- colnames(cand3) <- c("axis","snp","loading")

cand <- rbind(cand1, cand2, cand3)
cand$snp <- as.character(cand$snp)

foo <- matrix(nrow=(ncand), ncol=5)  # 5 columns for 5 predictors
colnames(foo) <- c("bio5","bio6","bio19","bio17","bio2")

for (i in 1:length(cand$snp)) {
  nam <- cand[i,2]
  snp.gen <- EU_genos.imp[,nam]
  foo[i,] <- apply(predictors,2,function(x) cor(x,snp.gen))
}

cand <- cbind.data.frame(cand,foo) 
cand_EU <- cand

# check which of the predictors each SNP is most strongly correlated with
for (i in 1:length(cand$snp)) {
  bar <- cand[i,]
  cand[i,9] <- names(which.max(abs(bar[4:8]))) # gives the variable
  cand[i,10] <- max(abs(bar[4:8]))              # gives the correlation
}

colnames(cand)[9] <- "predictor"
colnames(cand)[10] <- "correlation"

Env_Predictors <- levels(as.factor(cand$predictor))
No_Snps <- as.numeric(table(cand$predictor))
piedata <- data.frame(Env_Predictors,No_Snps)

# pie chart 
ggplot(piedata, aes(x="", y=No_Snps, fill=Env_Predictors)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c('#1f78b4','#33a02c','#e31a1c','#ffff33','gold')) +
  geom_col(color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = No_Snps),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5)) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  ggtitle("Number of candidate SNPs per environmental predictor") +
  theme_void()

# plot!
sel <- cand$snp
env <- cand$predictor
env[env=="bio5"] <- '#1f78b4'
env[env=="bio6"] <- '#33a02c'
env[env=="bio19"] <- '#e31a1c'
env[env=="bio17"] <- '#ffff33'
env[env=="bio2"] <- 'gold'
                
# color by predictor:
col.pred <- rownames(WUS.rda$CCA$v) # pull the SNP names
              
for (i in 1:length(sel)) {           # color code candidate SNPs
  foo <- match(sel[i],col.pred)
  col.pred[foo] <- env[i]
}
              
col.pred[grep("X",col.pred)] <- '#f1eef6' # non-candidate SNPs
empty <- col.pred
empty[grep("#f1eef6",empty)] <- rgb(0,1,0, alpha=0) # transparent
empty.outline <- ifelse(empty=="#00FF0000","#00FF0000","gray32")
bg <- c('#e31a1c','gold','red4','#ffff33','#1f78b4','#33a02c')

# axes 1 & 2
plot(EU.rda, type="n", scaling=3, xlim=c(-1,1), ylim=c(-1,1))
points(EU.rda, display="species", pch=21, cex=1.3, col="gray32", bg=col.pred, scaling=3)
```

Here, we compare the two lists to see if the same loci are invovled in response to climate in both range.
**Summary**: There are 79 candidates in the Western US RDA and 60 candidates in Turkey + Greece RDA, with 1 shared candidate locus. 

```{r}
# Verify the length of each set of candidate SNPs 
length(unique(cand_EU$snp)) #1037
length(unique(cand_WUS$snp)) #1019

display_venn <- function(x, ...){
  library(VennDiagram)
  grid.newpage()
  venn_object <- venn.diagram(x, filename = NULL, ...)
  grid.draw(venn_object)
}

ven <- list(cand.rda_EU = cand_EU$snp, cand.rda_WUS = cand_WUS$snp)

display_venn(ven, category.names = c("E. Europe" , "W. USA"),fill = c("blue", "red"))

rda_shared <- cand_EU$snp[cand_EU$snp %in% cand_WUS$snp]
```

## pRDA: Partial Redundancy Analysis 

The Partial Redundancy Analysis (pRDA) incorporates population structure to condition the RDA. Here, we use the first two PC axes to condition the RDA. This is likely very important for the native range, since there is lot of differentiation between the populations in Greece and Turkey. 

### Western United States 

**Summary**: There is very little population structure in the introduced range (Western US), and not much of this variation is explained by the first two PC axes (<3%). In total, there were 345 candidate SNPs, and there is much more equal splitting of candidate SNPs associated with bioclim variables: bio19 (Precipitation of Coldest Quarter, 84 SNPs), bio5 (Max Temperature of Warmest Month, 84 SNPs), bio2 (Mean Diurnal Range, 73 SNPs), bio17 (Precipitation of Driest Quarter, 68 SNPs), and bio6 (Min Temperature of Coldest Month, 36 SNPs). 

```{r}
library(vcfR)
library(adegenet)

WUS_vcf <- read.vcfR("introduced.populations.snps.thinned.1SD-removed.noLAFI.maf0.01.NoExHet.recode.vcf")
popmap3 <- read.delim("samples_to_keep.txt", sep = " ")
WUS_samples <- popmap3 %>% 
  dplyr::filter(V3 == "WesternUS")

genind <- vcfR2genind(WUS_vcf)
pop(genind) <- WUS_samples$V4
genind

# Run PCA after dealing with missing data, replace missing data with mean value for PC 
genind.nomissing <- tab(genind, freq=TRUE, NA.method="mean")
WUS_pca <- dudi.pca(genind.nomissing, center = T, scale = F, nf = 50, scannf = F)
s.class(WUS_pca$li, fac=pop(genind), col=funky(15), axesell = F, clabel = 0.5)
add.scatter.eig(WUS_pca$eig[1:25], 3, 1, 2, ratio = 0.25)

pve <- data.frame(PC=1:201,pve =WUS_pca$eig/sum(WUS_pca$eig)*100)
cumsum(pve$pve)
ggplot(data = pve, mapping =aes(x=PC, y=pve)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity") + xlim(0,50)

WUS_pcs <- WUS_pca$li
WUS_pop_str <- subset(WUS_pcs, select = c(Axis1, Axis2))

# load in dataframe with pop env vars for each individual for the individual-based GEA
env <- read.delim("individual_climate_data_30s.txt", sep = " ")
env$Site <- as.character(env$Site)

# Filter for individuals/pops in the GEA dataset 
locations <- read.delim("EUVI_locations.txt", header =T)
# Filter locations to only samples that we are using: 
popmap3 <- read.delim("samples_to_keep.txt", sep = " ")
locations_update <- distinct(locations[locations$EUVI_Sample %in% popmap3$V1,])

# Filter to all samples we are keeping: 
env <- env[env$EUVI_Sample %in% locations_update$EUVI_Sample,]


env_WUS <- env %>% 
  dplyr::filter(Long < 0) %>% 
  dplyr::select(EUVI_Sample, Site, Lat, Long, bio5, bio6, bio19, bio17, bio2) %>% 
  arrange(EUVI_Sample)
predictors <- env_WUS[,5:9]
# We need to make sure that samples are in the same order in both dfs...
WUS_pred_str <- cbind(predictors, WUS_pop_str) 

# run the pRDA
WUS.prda <- rda(WUS_genos.imp ~ + bio5 + bio6 + bio19 + 
                 bio17 + bio2 +
                 Condition(Axis1+Axis2), WUS_pred_str)
WUS.prda

# print eigenvalue summary and plot it
summary(eigenvals(WUS.prda, model = "constrained"))
screeplot(WUS.prda)

# axes 1 & 2
plot(WUS.prda, type="n", scaling=3)
points(WUS.prda, display="sites", pch=21, cex=1.75, col="black", scaling=3) 
text(WUS.prda, scaling=3, display="bp", col="black", cex=1.2)        

# axes 1 & 3
plot(WUS.prda, type="n", scaling=3, choices=c(1,3))
points(WUS.prda, display="sites", pch=21, cex=1.75, col="black", scaling=3, choices=c(1,3)) 
text(WUS.prda, scaling=3, display="bp", col="black", cex=1.2, choices=c(1,3))

# extract loadings of SNPs in ordination space
load.rda <- scores(WUS.prda, choices=c(1:3), display="species")

cand1 <- which(abs(load.rda[,1]) >= quantile(abs(load.rda[,1]), 0.9825))
cand2 <- which(abs(load.rda[,2]) >= quantile(abs(load.rda[,2]), 0.9834))
cand3 <- which(abs(load.rda[,3]) >= quantile(abs(load.rda[,3]), 0.9840))

# Total number of outlier SNPs
ncand <- length(cand1) + length(cand2) + length(cand3) #345 candidate snps in Western United States 

# make dataframe with candidate SNPs and correlations with each env variable
cand1 <- cbind.data.frame(rep(1,times=length(cand1)), names(cand1), unname(cand1))
cand2 <- cbind.data.frame(rep(2,times=length(cand2)), names(cand2), unname(cand2))
cand3 <- cbind.data.frame(rep(3,times=length(cand3)), names(cand3), unname(cand3))

colnames(cand1) <- colnames(cand2) <- colnames(cand3) <- c("axis","snp","loading")

cand <- rbind(cand1, cand2, cand3)
cand$snp <- as.character(cand$snp)

foo <- matrix(nrow=(ncand), ncol=5)  # 5 columns for 5 predictors
colnames(foo) <- c("bio5","bio6","bio19","bio17","bio2")

for (i in 1:length(cand$snp)) {
  nam <- cand[i,2]
  snp.gen <- WUS_genos.imp[,nam]
  foo[i,] <- apply(predictors,2,function(x) cor(x,snp.gen))
}

cand <- cbind.data.frame(cand,foo) 
prda.cand_WUS <- cand

# check which of the predictors each SNP is most strongly correlated with
for (i in 1:length(cand$snp)) {
  bar <- cand[i,]
  cand[i,9] <- names(which.max(abs(bar[4:8]))) # gives the variable
  cand[i,10] <- max(abs(bar[4:8]))              # gives the correlation
}

colnames(cand)[9] <- "predictor"
colnames(cand)[10] <- "correlation"

Env_Predictors <- levels(as.factor(cand$predictor))
No_Snps <- as.numeric(table(cand$predictor))
piedata <- data.frame(Env_Predictors,No_Snps)

# pie chart 
ggplot(piedata, aes(x="", y=No_Snps, fill=Env_Predictors)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c('#1f78b4','#33a02c','#e31a1c','#ffff33','gold')) +
  geom_col(color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = No_Snps),
```

### Europe (Turkey and Greece)

**Summary**: There is more population structure in the native range (Turkey + Greece), and an ok proportion of this variation is explained by the first two PC axes (~10%). In total, there were 363 candidate SNPs, and there is much more equal splitting of candidate SNPs associated with bioclim variables: bio6 (Min Temperature of Coldest Month, 76 SNPs), bio17 (Precipitation of Driest Quarter, 83 SNPs), bio5 (Max Temperature of Warmest Month, 78 SNPs), bio2 (Mean Diurnal Range, 75 SNPs), bio19 (Precipitation of Coldest Quarter, 51 SNPs). Note that this is nearly the opposite order compared to the introduced range!
```{r}

genind

s.class(EU_pca$li, fac=pop(genind), col=funky(15), axesell = F, clabel = 0.5)
add.scatter.eig(EU_pca$eig[1:25], 3, 1, 2, ratio = 0.25)
```

## LFMM: LFMM is a univariate test, which means that it builds a model for each SNP and each predictor variable.
From: https://bookdown.org/hhwagner1/LandGenCourse_book/WE_11.html

We first have to determine the optimal K value - we will use a PCA on the genomic data and compare to the 'broken stick criterion'. The LFMM is a univariate test, so we can't do an analysis on all 5 bioclim variables at one time, unless we do a PCA on them and then use the first PC axis in the analysis. However, we want to be able to compare these results to the pRDA results, so we will do a LFMM for each bioclim variable in each range (5 bioclim vars x 2 ranges = 10 total LFMM tests). Since within each LFMM analysis, every SNP is being tested against the environmental variable, we need to adjust the p-values using a false discovery rate (FDR) correction and can assess the calibration by looking at the genomic inflation factor (GIF), where a GIF close to 1 indicates an appropriately calibrated test.  

### Western United States:
**Summary**: We will use K=1 for the Western US since there is very little population structure in the PCA. There were a total of 6 SNPs with q-values < 0.1 after correcting for False Discovery Rate. 5 of these SNPs are associated with Bio2, and one is associatd with Bio19.  

- Bio5: 
  - GIF = 1.132, close to 1
  - #SNPS w/ P-value < 0.01 = 63
  - #SNPS w/ Q-value < 0.1 = 0
- Bio6: 
  - GIF = 1.577, elevated 
  - #SNPS w/ P-value < 0.01 = 61
  - #SNPS w/ Q-value < 0.1 = 0
- Bio2: 
  - GIF = 1.20, slightly elevated 
  - #SNPS w/ P-value < 0.01 = 99
  - #SNPS w/ Q-value < 0.1 = 5
- Bio17: 
  - GIF = 1.57, elevated
  - #SNPS w/ P-value < 0.01 = 64
  - #SNPS w/ Q-value < 0.1 = 0
- Bio19: 
  - GIF = 1.25, elevated 
  - #SNPS w/ P-value < 0.01 = 69
  - #SNPS w/ Q-value < 0.1 = 1


```{r}
# load in dataframe with pop env vars for each individual for the individual-based GEA
env <- read.delim("individual_climate_data_30s.txt", sep = " ")
env$Site <- as.character(env$Site)

# Filter for individuals/pops in the GEA dataset 
locations <- read.delim("EUVI_locations.txt", header =T)
# Filter locations to only samples that we are using: 
popmap3 <- read.delim("samples_to_keep.txt", sep = " ")
locations_update <- distinct(locations[locations$EUVI_Sample %in% popmap3$V1,])

# Filter to all samples we are keeping: 
env <- env[env$EUVI_Sample %in% locations_update$EUVI_Sample,]

# Now filter to only include samples in the introduced range and only the variables we are interested in
env_WUS <- env %>% 
  dplyr::filter(Long < 0) %>% 
  dplyr::select(EUVI_Sample, Site, Lat, Long, bio5, bio6, bio19, bio17, bio2) %>% 
  arrange(EUVI_Sample)
predictors <- env_WUS[,5:9]

# Prepare genotype data
WUS_genos <- read.table("introduced.populations.snps.thinned.1SD-removed.noLAFI.maf0.01.NoExHet.plink.raw", header = T, sep =" ", row.names=1)
dim(WUS_genos)

# extract genotypes from dataframe for prelim analysis
WUS_genos_only <- WUS_genos[,6:7092]

# calculate amount of missing data
sum(is.na(WUS_genos_only))/(7087*202) # the denominator is the sites*N

# fill missing values (NAs) with overall average for allele frequency variation
WUS_genos.imp <- apply(WUS_genos_only, 2, function(x) replace(x, is.na(x), as.numeric(names(which.max(table(x))))))
# double check that there are no longer any NA values
sum(is.na(WUS_genos.imp)) 
# genotype data is ready! 

# Need to make sure that predictors are in the same order as the genotype data! 
# I fixed this by arranging by the sample name prior to generating the predictor dataframe

#WUS.pca <- rda(WUS_genos.imp, scale = T)
#screeplot(WUS.pca, main = "Screeplot of RDA with Broken Stick", bstick = T, type = "barplot")

K <- 1


# LFMM on BIO5 
WUS.lfmm.bio5 <- lfmm_ridge(Y=WUS_genos.imp, X=env_WUS$bio5, K = K)

WUS.lfmm.bio5.test <- lfmm_test(Y=WUS_genos.imp, X=env_WUS$bio5, lfmm = WUS.lfmm.bio5, calibrate = "gif")
WUS.lfmm.bio5.test$gif

hist(WUS.lfmm.bio5.test$pvalue[,1], main = "Unadjusted P-values")
hist(WUS.lfmm.bio5.test$calibrated.pvalue[,1], main = "GIF-Adjusted P-Values")

length(which(WUS.lfmm.bio5.test$calibrated.pvalue< 0.01)) #129

# Convert the p-values into q-values, which are a measure of each SNP's significance after accounting for the FDR correction
WUS.lfmm.bio5.test.qv <- qvalue(WUS.lfmm.bio5.test$calibrated.pvalue)$qvalues
length(which(WUS.lfmm.bio5.test.qv < 0.1)) #0


# LFMM on BIO6
WUS.lfmm.bio6 <- lfmm_ridge(Y=WUS_genos.imp, X=env_WUS$bio6, K = K)

WUS.lfmm.bio6.test <- lfmm_test(Y=WUS_genos.imp, X=env_WUS$bio6, lfmm = WUS.lfmm.bio6, calibrate = "gif")
WUS.lfmm.bio6.test$gif # this is slightly elevated, 1.577

hist(WUS.lfmm.bio6.test$pvalue[,1], main = "Unadjusted P-values")
hist(WUS.lfmm.bio6.test$calibrated.pvalue[,1], main = "GIF-Adjusted P-Values")

length(which(WUS.lfmm.bio6.test$calibrated.pvalue< 0.01)) #61

# Convert the p-values into q-values, which are a measure of each SNP's significance after accounting for the FDR correction
WUS.lfmm.bio6.test.qv <- qvalue(WUS.lfmm.bio6.test$calibrated.pvalue)$qvalues
length(which(WUS.lfmm.bio6.test.qv < 0.1)) #0


# LFMM on BIO2
WUS.lfmm.bio2 <- lfmm_ridge(Y=WUS_genos.imp, X=env_WUS$bio2, K = K)

WUS.lfmm.bio2.test <- lfmm_test(Y=WUS_genos.imp, X=env_WUS$bio2, lfmm = WUS.lfmm.bio2, calibrate = "gif")
WUS.lfmm.bio2.test$gif # this is slightly elevated, but not too bad, 1.20

hist(WUS.lfmm.bio2.test$pvalue[,1], main = "Unadjusted P-values")
hist(WUS.lfmm.bio2.test$calibrated.pvalue[,1], main = "GIF-Adjusted P-Values")

length(which(WUS.lfmm.bio2.test$calibrated.pvalue< 0.01)) #99

# Convert the p-values into q-values, which are a measure of each SNP's significance after accounting for the FDR correction
WUS.lfmm.bio2.test.qv <- qvalue(WUS.lfmm.bio2.test$calibrated.pvalue)$qvalues
length(which(WUS.lfmm.bio2.test.qv < 0.1)) #5


# LFMM on BIO17
WUS.lfmm.bio17 <- lfmm_ridge(Y=WUS_genos.imp, X=env_WUS$bio17, K = K)

WUS.lfmm.bio17.test <- lfmm_test(Y=WUS_genos.imp, X=env_WUS$bio17, lfmm = WUS.lfmm.bio17, calibrate = "gif")
WUS.lfmm.bio17.test$gif # this is elevated, 1.57

hist(WUS.lfmm.bio17.test$pvalue[,1], main = "Unadjusted P-values")
hist(WUS.lfmm.bio17.test$calibrated.pvalue[,1], main = "GIF-Adjusted P-Values")

length(which(WUS.lfmm.bio17.test$calibrated.pvalue< 0.01)) #64

# Convert the p-values into q-values, which are a measure of each SNP's significance after accounting for the FDR correction
WUS.lfmm.bio17.test.qv <- qvalue(WUS.lfmm.bio17.test$calibrated.pvalue)$qvalues
length(which(WUS.lfmm.bio17.test.qv < 0.1)) #0


# LFMM on BIO19
WUS.lfmm.bio19 <- lfmm_ridge(Y=WUS_genos.imp, X=env_WUS$bio19, K = K)

WUS.lfmm.bio19.test <- lfmm_test(Y=WUS_genos.imp, X=env_WUS$bio19, lfmm = WUS.lfmm.bio19, calibrate = "gif")
WUS.lfmm.bio19.test$gif # this is slightly elevated, but not too bad, 1.25

# bio19
t <- as.data.frame(WUS.lfmm.bio19.test.qv)
```

```{r}
EU_genos <- read.table("native.populations.snps.thinned.1SD-removed.noLAFI.maf0.01.NoExHet.plink.raw", header = T, sep =" ", row.names=1)
dim(EU_genos)

# extract genotypes from dataframe for prelim analysis
EU_genos_only <- EU_genos[,6:7092]

# calculate amount of missing data
sum(is.na(EU_genos_only))/(7087*101) # the denominator is the sites*N

# fill missing values (NAs) with overall average for allele frequency variation
EU_genos.imp <- apply(EU_genos_only, 2, function(x) replace(x, is.na(x), as.numeric(names(which.max(table(x))))))
# double check that there are no longer any NA values
sum(is.na(EU_genos.imp)) 
# genotype data is ready!

# I fixed this by aranging by the sample name prior to generating the predictor dataframe

#EU.pca <- rda(EU_genos.imp, scale = T)

# LFMM on BIO5
```

## GF-RAW: Gradient Forest (GF) is a machine-learning approach to identify outliers in genomic datasets associated with environmental variables. We will also use some functions from Fitzpatrick et al. 2021. This approach uses the raw population allele frequencies without correcting for population structure in the dataset. 

### Western US:
**Summary**: 


```{r, warning=FALSE}
# These libraries were a pain to install on Mac w/ Apple chip. Had to reset the compiler path variables to 
# homebrew path and then it worked okay. 

#install.packages("~/Downloads/extendedForest_1.6.2.tar.gz", repos = NULL, type = "source")
#install.packages("~/Downloads/gradientForest_0.1-37.tar.gz", repo = NULL, type = "source")

library(gradientForest)

# Set path for allele frequency data. For this: should be a .csv with the populations across the top row and each is a SNP with the frequency of that SNP for a population in the corresponding cell 
library(vcfR)
library(adegenet)

WUS_vcf <- read.vcfR("introduced.populations.snps.thinned.1SD-removed.noLAFI.maf0.01.NoExHet.recode.vcf")
popmap3 <- read.delim("samples_to_keep.txt", sep = " ")
WUS_samples <- popmap3 %>% 
  dplyr::filter(V3 == "WesternUS")

genind <- vcfR2genind(WUS_vcf)
pop(genind) <- WUS_samples$V2
genind

# Convert genind to genpop, so that we can calculate the allele freqs for each population! 
genpop <- genind2genpop(genind)
allele.freq.WUS <- as.data.frame(makefreq(genpop))
colnames(allele.freq.WUS) <- make.names(colnames(allele.freq.WUS))
t.allele.freq.WUS <- as.data.frame(t(allele.freq.WUS))
# Add a new column for allele name
t.allele.freq.WUS$allele.name <- rownames(t.allele.freq.WUS)
# Get a summary column that has the overall frequency of the allele for each row
t.allele.freq.WUS <- mutate(t.allele.freq.WUS, overall.freq = rowMeans(t.allele.freq.WUS[,-82]))
# Remove the last two characters of the allele name in the dataframe 
t.allele.freq.WUS$allele.name <-substr(t.allele.freq.WUS$allele.name,1,nchar(t.allele.freq.WUS$allele.name)-2)
# Retain the allele that represents the minor allele frequency for each locus 
t.allele.freq.dedup.WUS <- t.allele.freq.WUS %>% 
  group_by(allele.name) %>% 
  arrange(overall.freq) %>% 
  filter(row_number() == 1)

t.allele.freq.dedup.WUS.onlyfreq <- t.allele.freq.dedup.WUS %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  dplyr::select(-c(allele.name, overall.freq))

WUS.allele.freq <- t(t.allele.freq.dedup.WUS.onlyfreq) 
colnames(WUS.allele.freq) <- t.allele.freq.dedup.WUS$allele.name

# Get environmental data. We will continue to use the 'env' object for this. The object should be a row for each population and a column for each variable, so we will get the mean value for each bioclim variable for each population (should actually be the same)

env <- read.delim("individual_climate_data_30s.txt", sep = " ")
env$Site <- as.character(env$Site)

# Filter for individuals/pops in the GEA dataset 
locations <- read.delim("EUVI_locations.txt", header =T)
# Filter locations to only samples that we are using: 
popmap3 <- read.delim("samples_to_keep.txt", sep = " ")
locations_update <- distinct(locations[locations$EUVI_Sample %in% popmap3$V1,])

# Filter to all s <- amples we are keeping: 
env <- env[env$EUVI_Sample %in% locations_update$EUVI_Sample,]

# Now filter to only include samples in the introduced range and only the variables we are interested in
env_WUS <- env %>% 
  dplyr::filter(Long < 0) %>% 
  dplyr::select(EUVI_Sample, Site, Lat, Long, bio5, bio6, bio19, bio17, bio2) %>% 
  arrange(EUVI_Sample) %>% 
  dplyr::select(Site, bio5, bio6, bio19, bio17, bio2) %>% 
  distinct()

colnames(env_WUS) <- c("pop_code", "bio5", "bio6", "bio19", "bio17", "bio2")

#b.env_WUS <- env_WUS %>% 
#  select(-c(pop_code))
#write.table(file = "env_WUS.txt", b.env_WUS, quote = F, row.names = F, col.names = F, sep = "\t")

# Names of variables used in fitting GF
predictors <- c("bio5", "bio6", "bio19", "bio17", "bio2")

# In GF, the maximum number of splits is defined by the following according to the suggestions of the authors:
maxLevel <- log2(0.368*nrow(env_WUS)/2)

# Now, run the GF model

gfSNPs.WUS <- gradientForest(cbind(WUS.allele.freq , env_WUS), predictor.vars = predictors, 
               response.vars = colnames(WUS.allele.freq), ntree = 500, maxLevel = maxLevel,
               trace = T, corr.threshold = 0.5)

plot(gfSNPs.WUS, plot.type = "Overall.Importance")
plot(gfSNPs.WUS, plot.type = "Split.Density")

# Now we can extract the importance (R2) values and format as table. We have to do this manually, 
# since the function only works on a modified GF output when each SNP is run independently. We 
# want to get a data.frame with a row for each SNP with R2 > 0 and a column with the R2 for each 
# predictor variable. 

gfSNPs.R2.WUS <- t(gfSNPs.WUS$imp.rsq) # 721 SNPs w/ R2 > 0 

Perc <- quantile(gfSNPs.R2.WUS, 0.95)

# Now I need to get the names of these outlier SNPs (138 SNPs)
gf.SNPs.R2.WUS.df <- as.data.frame(gfSNPs.R2.WUS)
gf.SNPs.R2.WUS.df.outliers <- gf.SNPs.R2.WUS.df %>% 
  filter(bio5 >= 0.04106876 | bio6 >= 0.04106876 | bio17 >= 0.04106876 | bio19 >= 0.04106876 | bio2 >= 0.04106876)

maxColumnNames <- as.data.frame(apply(gf.SNPs.R2.WUS.df.outliers, 1, function(row) colnames(gf.SNPs.R2.WUS.df.outliers)[which.max(row)]))

GFRaw.WUS.cand <- rownames(gf.SNPs.R2.WUS.df.outliers)

```

## BAYENV2: Here, we will analyze and assess the results from BAYENV2, a Bayesian model approach that calculates standardized allele frequencies that account for population history and relatedness in an attempt to adjust when detecting loci invovled in local adaptation.    

## Western US
**Summary**: 

```{r}
# We first need to standardize the environmental data for each range by subtracting the mean value and dividing by the standard deviation. I am doing this within each range, but not sure if that is the correct thing to do... 

env <- read.delim("individual_climate_data_30s.txt", sep = " ")
env$Site <- as.character(env$Site)

# Filter for individuals/pops in the GEA dataset 
locations <- read.delim("EUVI_locations.txt", header =T)
# Filter locations to only samples that we are using: 
popmap3 <- read.delim("samples_to_keep.txt", sep = " ")
locations_update <- distinct(locations[locations$EUVI_Sample %in% popmap3$V1,])

# Filter to all s <- amples we are keeping: 
env <- env[env$EUVI_Sample %in% locations_update$EUVI_Sample,]

# Now filter to only include samples in the introduced range and only the variables we are interested in
env_WUS <- env %>% 
  dplyr::filter(Long < 0) %>% 
  dplyr::select(EUVI_Sample, Site, Lat, Long, bio5, bio6, bio19, bio17, bio2) %>% 
  arrange(EUVI_Sample) %>% 
  dplyr::select(Site, bio5, bio6, bio19, bio17, bio2) %>% 
  distinct()

colnames(env_WUS) <- c("pop_code", "bio5", "bio6", "bio19", "bio17", "bio2")

sdize.env_WUS <- env_WUS %>% 
  dplyr::select(-c(pop_code)) %>% 
  mutate(sdize.bio5 = (bio5 - mean(bio5))/sd(bio5)) %>% 
  mutate(sdize.bio6 = (bio6 - mean(bio6))/sd(bio6)) %>% 
  mutate(sdize.bio19 = (bio19 - mean(bio19)/sd(bio19))) %>% 
  mutate(sdize.bio17 = (bio17 - mean(bio17)/sd(bio17))) %>% 
  mutate(sdize.bio2 = (bio2 - mean(bio2)/sd(bio2))) %>% 
  dplyr::select(sdize.bio5, sdize.bio6, sdize.bio19, sdize.bio17, sdize.bio2) %>% 
  t()

write.table(file = "standized.env_WUS.txt", sdize.env_WUS, quote = F, row.names = F, col.names = F, sep = "\t")

# Read in four independent covariance matrices to make sure they are well-correlated 
intro.matrix1 <- as.matrix(read.table("bayenv/introduced.last.matrix.chain1", header = F))
intro.matrix2 <- as.matrix(read.table("bayenv/introduced.last.matrix.chain2", header = F))
intro.matrix3 <- as.matrix(read.table("bayenv/introduced.last.matrix.chain3", header = F))
intro.matrix4 <- as.matrix(read.table("bayenv/introduced.last.matrix.chain4", header = F))

intro.matrix1.cor <- cor(intro.matrix1); heatmap(intro.matrix1.cor)
intro.matrix2.cor <- cor(intro.matrix2); heatmap(intro.matrix2.cor)
intro.matrix3.cor <- cor(intro.matrix3); heatmap(intro.matrix3.cor)
intro.matrix4.cor <- cor(intro.matrix4); heatmap(intro.matrix4.cor)

list <- list(intro.matrix1, intro.matrix2, intro.matrix3, intro.matrix4)

intro.matrix.mean <- Reduce("+", list) / length(list)
intro.matrix.mean.cor <- cor(intro.matrix.mean); heatmap(intro.matrix.mean.cor)

write.table(x = intro.matrix.mean, "bayenv/introduced.matrix.mean", row.names = F, col.names = F, quote = F, sep = "\t")

# Read in *.BF files from bayenv after running on command line

WUS_snp_names <- read.delim("bayenv/introduced.bayenv.snp.names_loci.txt", header = F)

WUS_BF1 <- as.matrix(read.delim("bayenv/introduced.chain1.bf", header = F, row.names = 1))
WUS_BF2 <- as.matrix(read.delim("bayenv/introduced.chain2.bf", header = F, row.names = 1))
WUS_BF3 <- as.matrix(read.delim("bayenv/introduced.chain3.bf", header = F, row.names = 1))
WUS_BF4 <- as.matrix(read.delim("bayenv/introduced.chain4.bf", header = F, row.names = 1))

WUS_BF_list <- list(WUS_BF1, WUS_BF2, WUS_BF3, WUS_BF4)

WUS_BF_mean <- as.data.frame(Reduce("+", WUS_BF_list) / length(WUS_BF_list))

cols <- c("bio5.BF", "bio6.BF", "bio19.BF", "bio17.BF", "bio2.BF", 
              "bio5.rho", "bio6.rho", "bio19.rho", "bio17.rho", "bio2.rho",
              "bio5.rs", "bio6.rs", "bio19.rs", "bio17.rs", "bio2.rs")

colnames(WUS_BF_mean) <- cols

WUS_BF_mean <- WUS_BF_mean %>% 
  mutate(abs.bio5.rho = abs(bio5.rho), abs.bio6.rho = abs(bio6.rho), 
         abs.bio19.rho = abs(bio19.rho), abs.bio17.rho = abs(bio17.rho), 
         abs.bio2.rho = abs(bio2.rho))

rownames(WUS_BF_mean) <- WUS_snp_names$V1

# Look at BAYES FACTORS first 

WUS_BF_mean.bf.mat <- as.matrix(dplyr::select(WUS_BF_mean, bio5.BF, bio6.BF, bio19.BF, bio17.BF, bio2.BF))

hist.data <- hist(WUS_BF_mean.bf.mat, breaks = 50, plot =F)
hist.data$counts = log10(hist.data$counts)
plot(hist.data, ylim = c(0, 5), xlim=c(0,20), xlab="bayenv2 BF values < 20", 
     ylab="log10(frequency)", main ="")
abline(v = 3)

length(which(WUS_BF_mean.bf.mat > 3)) #47 candidates w/ BF > 3

# Now look at RHO 

WUS_BF_mean.rho.mat <- as.matrix(dplyr::select(WUS_BF_mean, abs.bio5.rho, abs.bio6.rho, abs.bio19.rho, abs.bio17.rho, abs.bio2.rho))

hist.data <- hist(WUS_BF_mean.rho.mat, breaks = 50, plot =F)
hist.data$counts = log10(hist.data$counts)
plot(hist.data, ylim=c(0,6), xlim=c(0,1), xlab="bayenv2 rho values", 
     ylab="log10(frequency)", main ="")

# Now I need to get the names of these outlier SNPs -- 47 candidate loci 
WUS_BF.bf.outliers <- WUS_BF_mean %>% 
  filter(bio5.BF >= 3 | bio6.BF >= 3 | bio17.BF >= 3 | bio19.BF >= 3 | bio2.BF >= 3)

# Alternatively do the top 5% BFs and top 7% rhos -- this gives us 173 candidate loci 
BF.perc <- quantile(WUS_BF_mean.bf.mat, 0.95)
rho.perc <- quantile(WUS_BF_mean.rho.mat, 0.93)

WUS_BF.perc.outliers <- WUS_BF_mean %>% 
  mutate(class = case_when((bio5.BF >= BF.perc & abs.bio5.rho >= rho.perc) ~ "bio5_sig",
                           (bio6.BF >= BF.perc & abs.bio6.rho >= rho.perc) ~ "bio6_sig",
                           (bio19.BF >= BF.perc & abs.bio19.rho >= rho.perc) ~ "bio19_sig",
                           (bio17.BF >= BF.perc & abs.bio17.rho >= rho.perc) ~ "bio17_sig",
                           (bio2.BF >= BF.perc & abs.bio2.rho >= rho.perc) ~ "bio2_sig", TRUE ~ "not_sig")) %>% 
  filter(class != "not_sig")

# Doing it this way, by using percentiles, we get 173 significant candidates!  

WUS.Bayenv.cand <- rownames(WUS_BF.perc.outliers)

```

## GF-X: Gradient Forest (GF) is a machine-learning approach to identify outliers in genomic datasets associated with environmental variables. This approach uses standardized population allele frequencies by correcting for population structure in the dataset using bayenv-2.


## Western US
**Summary**: 

```{r}
WUS.stand.allele.freq <- read.delim("bayenv/introduced.snp.freq2", header =F)
t.WUS.stand.allele.freq <- as.data.frame(t(WUS.stand.allele.freq))

WUS.stand.allele.freq.snp_names <- read.delim("bayenv/introduced.bayenv.snp.names_loci.txt", header = F)

colnames(t.WUS.stand.allele.freq) <- make.names(WUS.stand.allele.freq.snp_names$V1)

rownames(t.WUS.stand.allele.freq) <- rownames(WUS.allele.freq)

# Get environmental data. We will continue to use the 'env' object for this. The object should be a row for each population and a column for each variable, so we will get the mean value for each bioclim variable for each population (should actually be the same)

env <- read.delim("individual_climate_data_30s.txt", sep = " ")
env$Site <- as.character(env$Site)

# Filter for individuals/pops in the GEA dataset 
locations <- read.delim("EUVI_locations.txt", header =T)
# Filter locations to only samples that we are using: 
popmap3 <- read.delim("samples_to_keep.txt", sep = " ")
locations_update <- distinct(locations[locations$EUVI_Sample %in% popmap3$V1,])

# Filter to all s <- amples we are keeping: 
env <- env[env$EUVI_Sample %in% locations_update$EUVI_Sample,]

# Now filter to only include samples in the introduced range and only the variables we are interested in
env_WUS <- env %>% 
  dplyr::filter(Long < 0) %>% 
  dplyr::select(EUVI_Sample, Site, Lat, Long, bio5, bio6, bio19, bio17, bio2) %>% 
  arrange(EUVI_Sample) %>% 
  dplyr::select(Site, bio5, bio6, bio19, bio17, bio2) %>% 
  distinct()

colnames(env_WUS) <- c("pop_code", "bio5", "bio6", "bio19", "bio17", "bio2")

# Names of variables used in fitting GF
predictors <- c("bio5", "bio6", "bio19", "bio17", "bio2")

# In GF, the maximum number of splits is defined by the following according to the suggestions of the authors:
maxLevel <- log2(0.368*nrow(env_WUS)/2)

# Now, run the GF model

gfX.SNPs.WUS <- gradientForest(cbind(t.WUS.stand.allele.freq, env_WUS), predictor.vars = predictors, 
               response.vars = colnames(t.WUS.stand.allele.freq), ntree = 500, maxLevel = maxLevel,
               trace = T, corr.threshold = 0.5)


plot(gfX.SNPs.WUS, plot.type = "Overall.Importance")
plot(gfX.SNPs.WUS, plot.type = "Split.Density")

# Now we can extract the importance (R2) values and format as table. We have to do this manually, 
# since the function only works on a modified GF output when each SNP is run independently. We 
# want to get a data.frame with a row for each SNP with R2 > 0 and a column with the R2 for each 
# predictor variable. 

gfX.SNPs.R2.WUS <- t(gfX.SNPs.WUS$imp.rsq) #10 SNPs w/ R2 > 0 

Perc <- quantile(gfX.SNPs.R2.WUS, 0.95)

# Now I need to get the names of these outlier SNPs: 
gfX.SNPs.R2.WUS.df <- as.data.frame(gfX.SNPs.R2.WUS)
gfX.SNPs.R2.WUS.df.outliers <- gfX.SNPs.R2.WUS.df %>% 
  filter(bio5 >= 0.03296629 | bio6 >= 0.03296629 | bio17 >= 0.03296629 | bio19 >= 0.03296629 | bio2 >= 0.03296629)

# There are 2 outlier SNPs
GFX.WUS.cand <- rownames(gfX.SNPs.R2.WUS.df.outliers)
```

To prevent having to re-do all the above multiple times, let's read in the previous results and re-format so we can make an Upset plot. The first Upset plot shows the introduced range and the second Upset plot shows the native range. 

```{r}
library(UpSetR)
full_candidates <- read.delim("full_candidate_list.txt", sep = " ")

RDA.WUS <- full_candidates %>% select(locus, RDA.WUS) %>%  na.omit() %>% select(locus)
pRDA.WUS <- full_candidates %>% select(locus, pRDA.WUS) %>%  na.omit() %>% select(locus)
gfRaw.WUS <- full_candidates %>% select(locus, gfRaw.WUS) %>%  na.omit() %>% select(locus)

LFMM.WUS <- full_candidates %>% select(locus, LFMM.WUS) %>% na.omit() %>% select(locus)

RDA.WUS <- as.vector(RDA.WUS$locus)
pRDA.WUS <- as.vector(pRDA.WUS$locus)
gfRaw.WUS <- as.vector(gfRaw.WUS$locus)
gfX.WUS <- as.vector(gfX.WUS$locus)
bayenv.WUS <- as.vector(bayenv.WUS$locus)
LFMM.WUS <- as.vector(LFMM.WUS$locus)

wus<- list(RDA = RDA.WUS, pRDA = pRDA.WUS, "Gradient Forest Raw" = gfRaw.WUS, "Gradient Forest X" = gfX.WUS, Bayenv = bayenv.WUS, LFMM = LFMM.WUS)

pdf(file="WUS_upset.pdf", onefile = F, width = 10) 
upset(fromList(wus), nsets = 6, text.scale = 2)
dev.off()
```

## Annotation of candidate loci
**Summary**: Here, I used blastx to identify sequence homology between the RAD loci and the <i>Euwallacea fornicatus</i> proteome (another weevil). I filtered to only include the best blast hit based on E-value and then searched against each of the candidate lists to see if the candidates had blast hits. 

```{r}
blast <- read.delim("populations.loci.blast", header = F)
colnames(blast) <- c("qseqid", "sseqid", "pident", "length", "mismatch", "gapopen", "qstart", "qend",
                     "sstart", "send", "evalue", "bitscore")

blast.filt <- blast %>% 
  group_by(qseqid) %>% 
  arrange(evalue) %>% 
  filter(row_number() == 1)

blast.filt <- lapply(blast.filt, function(x) as.character(gsub("CLocus_","", x)))
blast.filt <- as.data.frame(blast.filt)
blast.filt$locus <- blast.filt$qseqid
```
